standard.title: First Nations visual arts and Country/Place
standard.description: explore how First Nations Australians use visual arts to communicate their connection to and responsibility for Country/Place
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have explored artworks by First Nations Australians, identified visual conventions and observed how Country/Place is central to First Nations art-making (AC9AVA2E02). They understand that place is connected to identity. They have not yet explored the concept of responsibility for Country/Place, or examined how visual arts communicate this responsibility.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore how First Nations Australians use visual arts to communicate their connection to and responsibility for Country/Place.

nodes.label: Responsibility for Country/Place
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that First Nations Australian visual arts communicate not only connection to Country/Place but also responsibility for caring for it.
nodes.minimum_width: Look at one First Nations Australian artwork and identify at least one way it communicates responsibility or care for Country/Place (not only connection).
nodes.typical_width: Access accounts by contemporary First Nations Australian artists about their ideas concerning Country/Place; use Viewpoints questions to investigate what the works communicate about responsibility; discuss spiritual and intellectual connections to land, sea, sky and waterways.
wider: Explore visual arts that share cultural accounts of Country/Place — investigate how specific visual conventions, symbols and patterns communicate responsibility for specific places
Examine artworks addressing the diversity of First Nations Nations — investigate how distinct communities communicate their relationships to their own Country/Place
nodes.hinge_reason: The shift from connection to responsibility is the conceptual advance in this descriptor over Y1-2 — students who understand only connection miss the relational and ethical dimension that gives First Nations visual arts their full meaning at this level.

response_modes.reason: Responsibility for Country/Place is an unfamiliar concept for most students. Explicit discussion with targeted prompts is needed before students can identify it in artworks — the concept must be introduced before artworks can demonstrate it.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one way a First Nations Australian artwork communicates responsibility or care for Country/Place
Distinguishes between connection (belonging to a place) and responsibility (caring for a place)

nodes.label: Symbols, stories and cultural identity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine symbols and emblems important to First Nations Australians and understand their importance to identity and culture, engaging with people of cultural authority.
nodes.minimum_width: Examine at least one symbol or emblem important to First Nations Australians and explain what it communicates about identity or culture.
nodes.typical_width: Examine a diverse range of symbols and emblems; engage with accounts from people with cultural authority about their importance; explore artworks addressing cultural identity; connect visual conventions to specific cultural meanings.
wider: Explore visual conventions, symbols or patterns with representatives of a First Nations Australian community, or through resources created or co-created by First Nations Australians — document what you learn about how the visual conventions carry cultural meaning
Compare place-based symbols across different First Nations communities — investigate how different communities use visual conventions to communicate their specific relationships to their Country

response_modes.reason: Students who examine symbols from only one First Nations community risk homogenising First Nations culture. Engaging with diverse communities and their distinct symbols builds respect for cultural specificity.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The diversity of First Nations Australian symbols, emblems and visual conventions across distinct communities is genuinely rich — students who engage with this diversity gain a more accurate and respectful understanding than any single example allows.
success_criteria: Examines at least one symbol or emblem important to a First Nations Australian community
Explains what it communicates about identity or cultural connection, using information from culturally authoritative sources

nodes.label: Personal connections and visual arts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can reflect on their own cultural connections and consider how visual arts can communicate personal connection to place.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least one personal connection to a place (family, community, landscape) and one visual way to represent it.
nodes.typical_width: Map personal cultural connections — place, language, family customs, values — and use Viewpoints questions to plan an artwork that communicates connection to place; reflect on how First Nations Australian approaches to this question compare with your own.
wider: Create an artwork that communicates your personal connection to place using visual conventions meaningful to you — reflect on similarities and differences between your approach and approaches used by First Nations Australian artists
Investigate stories connected to local Country/Place — explore how knowledge of place history enriches the visual arts made in and about a place

response_modes.reason: This node brings together the conceptual understanding of Country/Place responsibility and the personal making dimension — students connect what they have learned about First Nations Australian visual arts to their own relationship with place.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one personal cultural connection to a place
Reflects on how First Nations Australian approaches to communicating place connection compare with how they would communicate their own
